workflow: Manually refreshing WhatsApp Cloud API access tokens every 24 hours because the API does not support automatic refresh or long-lived tokens for server-to-server communication.
trigger: Access token expires after 24 hours, causing API calls to fail with 401 errors.
current_workaround: Developers write cron jobs or scheduled tasks that call the token refresh endpoint manually, or they store refresh tokens and implement custom token rotation logic.
consequence: If the manual refresh fails or is missed, all WhatsApp API calls stop working, leading to message delivery failures and customer-facing issues.

workflow: Manually verifying webhook endpoints by repeatedly checking the challenge response and debugging cryptic error messages when the verification token does not match.
trigger: Setting up a webhook for the first time or after changing the endpoint URL.
current_workaround: Developers use tools like ngrok to test locally, constantly compare verification tokens, and manually resend verification requests from the Meta Developer portal.
consequence: Webhook setup failures block inbound message processing, delaying integration; multiple attempts waste developer hours.

workflow: Manually validating template parameters (e.g., {{1}}, {{2}}) to ensure correct formatting, localization, and escape sequences, especially for Chinese, Arabic, or special characters.
trigger: A new template is created or an existing template is edited, and the API rejects it with a vague error like 'parameter mismatch'.
current_workaround: Developers copy-paste template samples into separate validation tools, manually check character counts, and repeatedly submit to the API until it passes.
consequence: Template rejection blocks marketing campaigns or customer notifications; each failed attempt consumes time and delays rollout.

workflow: Manually scheduling WhatsApp messages (e.g., reminders, alerts) by writing custom cron jobs, managing time zones, and handling queue persistence because the API does not natively support scheduled sends.
trigger: Business requirement to send messages at a specific future time (e.g., appointment reminders).
current_workaround: Developers build internal schedulers using Redis or database tables, write scripts to poll and send at the right time, and handle retries manually.
consequence: Scheduling logic is fragile; time zone errors, server downtime, or queue corruption can cause missed messages, leading to customer complaints.

workflow: Manually iterating through contact lists, adding delays to avoid rate limits, and handling partial failures when sending bulk messages (e.g., promotions, alerts) because the API only supports single-message send.
trigger: Marketing or operational need to send the same message to many recipients.
current_workaround: Developers write scripts that loop over recipients, sleep between requests, log each response, and retry failures manually. Some use distributed queues to parallelize while respecting rate limits.
consequence: Bulk sends take hours; rate limit errors cause partial sends; manual reconciliation needed to identify which messages actually went through, creating operational overhead.
